title: For Diwali, Rachel Gurjar Serves Sticky Wings, Sweet Potato Chaat and Brûléed Kheer
excerpt: The Mumbai-raised, Brooklyn-based author's Bon Appétit menu — drawn from her debut cookbook East to East — is built for the open-house weeks before Diwali on November 8.
body:
• Bon Appétit has published Mumbai-raised, Brooklyn-based cookbook author Rachel Gurjar's Diwali menu, built around sticky chicken wings, a Japanese sweet potato chaat and a brûléed kheer with mango sorbet.
  • The menu appears a week before Diwali, which falls on November 8 this year, and draws on Gurjar's debut cookbook East to East, published October 13 with 101 Indian-inspired recipes.
  • Her green chutney for the chaat blends 2 bunches of cilantro, a bunch of mint, green chiles, lime juice, cumin, sugar and chaat masala; the kheer is slow-cooked from jasmine rice, whole milk, condensed milk, cardamom and cinnamon, then brûléed.
  • Gurjar frames the menu through memory: in her childhood home, the weeks before Diwali were led by her grandmother, mother and aunts, who cleaned the house and prepared snacks and sweets for a steady stream of guests.

Diwali hosting, in Rachel Gurjar's telling, is a season, not a dinner. "Growing up, I remember a steady stream of guests coming in and out of our home in the weeks leading up to Diwali," the Mumbai-raised, Brooklyn-based cookbook author writes in Bon Appétit, in a menu published November 1 ahead of Diwali on November 8. "The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga. Our celebrations were led by women, my grandmother, mother, and aunts, who would meticulously clean the house and spend weeks preparing snacks and sweets. They taught me the art of hosting and how to share the joy of food with our community."

What's on the menu

""The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga."

The spread Bon Appétit published is built for that kind of open-house eating. The headline dish is a plate of sticky chicken wings — party food, eaten with the hands, made to keep coming out of the kitchen. Alongside it, a Japanese sweet potato chaat: slow-roasted sweet potatoes topped with tamarind concentrate, green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes and cilantro. A homestyle chicken kari rounds out the savouries, simmering in onions, tomatoes and a heady mix of spices. Dessert is a brûléed kheer — rice pudding with a crackly caramelised top — served with a scoop of mango sorbet.

Two recipes worth stealing

The chaat's green chutney is the kind of recipe that earns its place in a Diwali kitchen, because it goes on everything. Gurjar blends 2 bunches of cilantro (about 6 oz, leaves and stems), 1 bunch of mint (about 2 oz), 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, half a cup of lime juice, 2 teaspoons of cumin seeds, 1½ teaspoons of fine sea salt, a teaspoon of sugar and a teaspoon of chaat masala, pulsing in intervals until it forms a smooth paste.

The kheer is a slow-cooked pudding of 5 cups of whole milk, a 14-oz can of sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, a cinnamon stick, 1 cup of jasmine rice and a quarter-teaspoon of fine sea salt — then finished with a brûléed sugar top and the mango sorbet. "This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom," Gurjar writes. "I'm serving it with a little twist here — a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor."

The chicken kari, meanwhile, is built on her mother's garam masala — bay leaves, cloves, black cardamom, star anise, cinnamon, nutmeg, coriander seeds, mace, cumin, black peppercorns and white poppy seeds, toasted briefly in a dry skillet. "This chicken kari recipe fills your house with the rich, comforting aroma of chicken simmering in a heady mix of spices, onions, and tomatoes," Bon Appétit's own description reads.

The book behind it

The menu arrives weeks after Gurjar's debut cookbook, East to East: Recipes and Stories from Mumbai to New York, which was published on October 13 with 101 Indian-inspired recipes alongside essays on migration, memory and making a home between cultures. The book was named among Bon Appétit's Best New Cookbooks of Fall 2026. For diaspora hosts planning their own Diwali table before November 8, her formula is the takeaway: one sticky, snackable centrepiece, one chaat, one homestyle curry, and a familiar dessert with one deliberate twist.
